505.title: To whom shall we go (John 6:60–69)
505.hook: many walk away; Peter says thou hast the words of eternal life
505.howItsDone: Catholics hear Peter's answer on the Twenty-first Sunday in Ordinary Time in Year B, the last of the Sundays that read through John 6.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the words the crowd argued over: my flesh is meat indeed. Your line was eat, and live. And a new week begins.

It ends in a synagogue in Capernaum, where John says Jesus taught all of it: the bread, the flesh, the blood. And it costs him. Not the hillside crowd this time: his own disciples, people who had been following him, start to leave. Some of them may have eaten the loaves by the lake. Jesus watches them go. He doesn't run after them with a softer version. Then he turns to the twelve still standing there and asks a question that leaves the door wide open.
screen: `A SYNAGOGUE IN CAPERNAUM.` → `HIS OWN DISCIPLES WALK OUT.` → `HE TURNS TO THE TWELVE.`

segments.voice: It starts with a complaint, in the Douay-Rheims: "This saying is hard, and who can hear it?" Not just hard to understand. Hard to accept. Jesus knows they're murmuring, and he doesn't take it back. His words, he says, are spirit and life, and some of them don't believe. Then: "After this many of his disciples went back; and walked no more with him." Jesus turns to the twelve: "Will you also go away?" Not a threat. A real question. He lets them choose. And Peter answers, first and from the gut: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." Notice what Peter doesn't say. Not, I understand it all now. Not, it isn't hard. Not even, I'm sure. Just: where else would we go? It's the faith of someone who has looked at the alternatives and can't walk away from these words. Then he adds: we have believed and have known that thou art the Christ, the Son of God. Some Catholics turn to this line on days when the teaching is hard, or the Church is hard to love, or God is silent. Staying isn't the same as having no questions. Peter will deny Jesus three times before the story ends. But here, when it costs something, he stays.

segments.voice: Think of something you're tempted to walk away from, a commitment, a friendship, a hard conversation, maybe even this path, and don't decide anything; just stay with it for now, noticing the urge to get up and go without following it. If you pray, use Peter's words, Lord, to whom shall we go; if not, notice what staying feels like.

506.title: Rivers of living water (John 7:37–39)
506.hook: on the feast's last day he stands and cries out
506.howItsDone: Catholics hear John 7:37–39 at the Vigil Mass of Pentecost, linking the rivers of living water to the gift of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Capernaum emptying out, and Peter staying anyway. Your line was words of eternal life.

Autumn in Jerusalem, and the city is full of huts. For the feast of Tabernacles, families build shelters of branches on rooftops and in courtyards and live in them for a week, remembering the years in the desert. It's a harvest festival, and a prayer for rain before the dry ground has to be planted. Each morning of the feast, according to the old Jewish sources, a priest carried water up from the pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher and poured it out at the altar, with trumpets and singing. On the last day, the great day, Jesus stands up and shouts.
screen: `A CITY FULL OF HUTS.` → `WATER POURED AT THE ALTAR.` → `ON THE LAST DAY, HE SHOUTS.`

segments.voice: John says he stood and cried out, a man on his feet, raising his voice over a festival crowd. In the Douay-Rheims: "If any man thirst, let him come to me, and drink." Then: "He that believeth in me, as the scripture saith, Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." Out of his belly sounds strange in English. The Greek word means the belly, the inside, the deepest part of a person; we'd say the heart, or the gut. We've heard living water before, at the well in Samaria. Here it isn't a cup. It's rivers. And John stops to tell us what it means: this he said of the Spirit, which those who believed in him were going to receive; the Spirit wasn't yet given, because Jesus wasn't yet glorified. So the water poured at the altar becomes a picture of something still to come. Here's an old puzzle: the sentence can be divided two ways. The Douay reads it as the believer's belly. But some early Christian writers read it as Christ's own: let the one who believes come and drink, for out of him flow rivers. Both readings have histories in the Church, and some readers hear them together: the Spirit flows from Christ, and then through the believer to others. John may be pointing ahead, too. At the cross, a soldier's spear opens Jesus's side, and blood and water come out. The Catechism sees the sacraments, and the Church itself, flowing from that wound.

segments.voice: Breathe in and notice something you've been given lately, a kindness, rest, an idea, time; breathe out slowly and picture some of it flowing on, past you, to someone else, because a river doesn't keep its water. If you pray, ask that what you've been given flow out; if not, just let one person come to mind who could use it.

507.title: The light of the world (John 8:12)
507.hook: whoever follows me walks not in darkness
507.tomorrow: The truth shall make you free
507.howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil Catholics light the paschal candle from a new fire and pass its flame to candles throughout the church, as the deacon sings "the light of Christ" three times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last day of Tabernacles and rivers of living water. Your line was out of his belly.

The Easter Vigil begins in the dark. The church is black. A single fire is lit outside, and from it one tall candle. A deacon carries it in and stops three times, lifting it and singing the same short phrase: the light of Christ. People light their small candles from it, and the light moves back through the church, hand to hand, until the whole building glows. What the candle proclaims goes back to one sentence Jesus spoke in the middle of an old feast of lamps. We're still at the feast of Tabernacles.
screen: `THE EASTER VIGIL IN THE DARK.` → `ONE CANDLE, THEN HUNDREDS.` → `BACK TO TABERNACLES.`

segments.voice: The feast had water, and it also had light. The Jewish sources describe great golden lampstands set up in the temple courts, so tall that young priests climbed ladders to fill them with oil. The wicks were made from the priests' worn-out garments. The old account says there wasn't a courtyard in Jerusalem that didn't shine with their light, and men danced with torches through the night. Jesus is teaching in the treasury, John says, right by that court. And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness, but shall have the light of life." It's the second great I am. Bread is what you need every day; light is what lets you see everything else. Notice the promise. He doesn't say there will be no darkness. He says the one who follows will not walk in it. Following is a walking word: a lamp held up ahead on a dark road. You still have to walk, but you can see where to put your feet. We heard this light at the start of the Gospel: the light shineth in darkness. In Matthew, Jesus turns it around: you are the light of the world. The Church holds both together: Christ is the light, and those who follow him carry it. That's the Easter Vigil in one gesture: one candle, then every hand passing the flame along.

segments.voice: Stand by a window or a lamp, or step outside into daylight, and walk slowly toward the light, feeling each step land. Notice how light changes what you see: edges, colors, faces, your own hands. If you pray, hold the line, he that followeth me walketh not in darkness; if not, just walk and notice the light.

508.title: The truth shall make you free (John 8:31–32)
508.word: The truth shall make you free
508.hook: freedom comes from continuing in his word
508.howItsDone: Catholics hear John 8:31–42 at a weekday Mass in the fifth week of Lent, and the Church's moral teaching, especially Saint John Paul II's Veritatis Splendor, draws on it to link freedom with truth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the golden lampstands of Tabernacles and the light of the world. Your line was not in darkness.

Still in the temple, still the same long argument, and John points to some people in the crowd who have just come to believe in him. A teacher might greet new followers with a welcome. Jesus gives them a sentence that starts with a condition: if. The second half is famous on its own, and on its own it can sound like a slogan about facts. Today, the whole sentence, and how fast these new believers start arguing about who is free.
screen: `NEW BELIEVERS IN THE TEMPLE.` → `A SENTENCE THAT STARTS WITH IF.` → `AN ARGUMENT ABOUT FREEDOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "If you continue in my word, you shall be my disciples indeed. And you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." It begins with if. If you continue: stay, remain, keep living in my word. Freedom doesn't come at the start; it comes from staying. And truth here isn't first of all a fact you look up. In John's Gospel, truth is close to a person: later Jesus will say, I am the way, and the truth, and the life. Catholic readers hear knowing the truth as coming to know him, over time, by staying. His listeners bristle. We are Abraham's children, they say, and we've never been slaves to anyone. Jesus answers that he means another kind of slavery: "whosoever committeth sin, is the servant of sin." The thing you can't stop doing. The lie you have to keep up. The habit that runs you. Then: if the Son makes you free, you shall be free indeed. Saint John Paul the Second's letter on moral life, The Splendor of Truth, keeps coming back to this verse. Freedom, he wrote, isn't doing whatever we like; it depends on truth and grows by living in it. Every lie needs guarding. Every truth you finally tell is one less thing to guard.

segments.voice: Let one small thing come to mind that you haven't said: I'm the one who broke it, I'm actually not fine, I liked your idea more than I said. Notice how much effort it takes to keep it unsaid, and picture saying it, plainly and kindly. If you pray, ask for the courage to say it; if not, just hold it there a moment.

509.title: Before Abraham was (John 8:58)
509.hook: before Abraham was made, I am
509.howItsDone: Catholics profess in the Nicene Creed at Sunday Mass that the Son is "begotten, not made," and hear John 8:51–59 at a weekday Mass in the fifth week of Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole sentence: if you continue in my word, the truth shall make you free. Your line was the truth sets free.

Before my grandmother was born, I am. A grammar teacher would circle that in red. The tenses don't match; it should be I was. Nobody says it this way. And yet that's the sentence at the end of John chapter eight, and the wrong tense is the point. The argument in the temple has been going on a long time, and getting hotter. It's about Abraham, the father of the people. And Jesus ends it with two words that make his listeners reach for stones.
screen: `A SENTENCE WITH THE WRONG TENSE.` → `AN ARGUMENT ABOUT ABRAHAM.` → `TWO WORDS, AND STONES.`

segments.voice: Jesus says that Abraham rejoiced to see his day; he saw it and was glad. His listeners answer, reasonably: you're not yet fifty years old, and you've seen Abraham? And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Amen, amen I say to you, before Abraham was made, I am." Listen to the two verbs. Abraham was made: he came into being at a point in time, like all of us. I am: not I was, not I came to be. Just is. The Church hears in it: no beginning. Why the stones? Readers connect it to a name. At the burning bush, Moses asked God's name, and the Douay-Rheims gives the answer: "I AM WHO AM." A man saying I am like that could be heard as claiming the name of God, which to a devout listener would be blasphemy. John doesn't spell out their reason. They take up stones; he hides himself and goes out of the temple. We met the Word who was in the beginning on the first day of this Gospel. This is the same claim, now in his own mouth. The Catholic Church reads it plainly: the Son is eternal, one in being with the Father, God from God. It's in the Creed every Sunday: begotten, not made. And the argument here isn't between Christians and Jews as we know them now. It's among Jewish people in the temple, with a Jewish teacher, over what God had revealed. The Church teaches that this conflict must never be used to blame the Jewish people as a whole.

segments.voice: On the in-breath, say silently, I; on the out-breath, am, slowly, again and again, adding nothing after it, not tired, not late, just I am. If you pray, hold the words as God's name, given at the bush and spoken in the temple; if not, rest in the plain fact of being here.

510.title: The man born blind (John 9:1–12)
510.hook: mud on the eyes, wash in Siloe, and he comes back seeing
510.howItsDone: Catholics hear the man born blind on the Fourth Sunday of Lent in Year A, used with the scrutinies for adults preparing for baptism at Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ego eimi, the wrong tense on purpose: before Abraham was made, I am. Your line was I am.

When something terrible happens, the question comes fast: whose fault is it? A child is born sick, and a relative wonders aloud what the parents did. It's an old reflex, and the disciples have it too. Walking along, they pass a man who has been blind since birth, begging by the road. And they ask Jesus, as if the man weren't there: Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind? Jesus refuses the question, and then he bends down to the dirt.
screen: `WHOSE FAULT IS IT?` → `A MAN BLIND FROM BIRTH.` → `WHO SINNED, HIM OR HIS PARENTS?`

segments.voice: His answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents; but that the works of God should be made manifest in him." Neither. He won't hand out blame. He doesn't explain why the man was born blind; the text never does. He turns the question from why did this happen to what will God do here. Then he says again what he said at the feast: as long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world. And he does something earthy. He spits on the ground, makes mud, and spreads it on the man's eyes. Some early Christian writers saw an echo of Genesis, where God shapes the first man from the dust: the one who made eyes in the beginning is making them again. Then: "Go, wash in the pool of Siloe, which is interpreted, Sent. He went therefore, and washed, and he came seeing." He isn't healed on the spot. He has to walk, blind, mud on his face, to the pool. Siloe, Siloam in other Bibles, means sent, and just before this Jesus has spoken of him that sent me. The pool's name points back at the one doing the healing. The early Church heard baptism in this story. Justin Martyr called baptism illumination, and the Church still reads this Gospel in Lent with adults preparing to be baptized at Easter.

segments.voice: If you can, go to a sink, or just cup your hands and imagine water in them, and bring it slowly to your face, over your eyes, holding your hands there a moment. Then open your eyes and look at what's in front of you as if for the first time. If you pray, ask to see clearly; if not, notice what washing feels like when you pay attention.

511.title: One thing I know (John 9:13–41)
511.hook: whereas I was blind, now I see
511.howItsDone: Catholics hear the whole of John 9, the trial as well as the healing, in the longer form of the Gospel on the Fourth Sunday of Lent in Year A.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Siloe, the pool called Sent, and a man who came back seeing. Your line was go, wash.

The man has barely begun to see when the questions start. He's questioned by religious authorities, then questioned again. His parents are summoned, and they're too frightened to speak for him. By the end he has been thrown out. The healing takes two verses; the argument about it fills the rest of the chapter, and it's mostly a trial. And the man who used to beg by the road turns out to have a sharp tongue.
screen: `FIRST, HE SEES.` → `THEN, THE QUESTIONS.` → `THEN, THROWN OUT.`

segments.voice: The healing happened on a Sabbath, and the Pharisees are divided. Some say a man who doesn't keep the Sabbath can't be from God; others ask how a sinner could do such signs. They call the man back and press him: give glory to God; we know this man is a sinner. He answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "If he be a sinner, I know not: one thing I know, that whereas I was blind, now I see." He doesn't argue theology or claim to know everything. He knows one thing, from the inside. When they ask him to tell it all again, he asks, with a straight face, whether they want to become his disciples too. Watch him grow through the chapter. At first, Jesus is the man that is called Jesus. Then a prophet. Then a man from God. They put him out, and Jesus, hearing of it, goes looking for him and asks if he believes in the Son of God. Who is he, Lord, that I may believe? You have seen him, Jesus says, and it is he that talketh with thee. "And he said: I believe, Lord. And falling down, he adored him." Some readers think the fear of being put out of the synagogue also reflects painful conflicts in the communities John was writing for. The Church reads the chapter as a story about sight that grows: the one who was blind sees more and more, and those sure they could see are asked whether they really do.
screen: `THE PHARISEES ARE DIVIDED.` · `ONE THING I KNOW.` · `A NAME, A PROPHET, FROM GOD, LORD.` · `I BELIEVE, LORD.` · then, large: `WHEREAS I WAS BLIND, NOW I SEE.`

segments.voice: Think back over the past few months, on this path or in your life, and find one thing you see now that you didn't before, about a person, about yourself, about God. Say it plainly to yourself, the way he did: whereas I was blind, now I see this. If you pray, give thanks for it; if not, just let it be named.
One thing I know. The healed man's answer to his questioners: I don't know everything, but whereas I was blind, now I see. Today's word.
Your line: now I see. That's week seventy-three: words of eternal life, rivers, light, truth, I am, Siloe, and one thing I know.
